criteria.pass: She drops it 8 out of 10 times without you moving toward her.

skills.title: Tug, with rules
skills.age: Gentle tug now. Real tug waits for her adult teeth, around six or seven months.
skills.sessions: 60 to 90 seconds, two or three times a day. Always ended by you.
skills.why: Tug is the best reward you own that is not food, and you will need it for recall later, when kibble stops outbidding another dog. It is the legal outlet for a retriever's mouth. And it is where DROP IT gets tested under real excitement, which is the only test that counts. Tug does not make a dog aggressive. A tug game with no rules makes a dog rude, and the rules are the entire point of the exercise.
need: A long soft tug toy, so her teeth are nowhere near your hand
DROP IT already working in a quiet room
The suction cup toy: yes, but read step 6 first

steps.do: You start it, always. Bring the toy out, wiggle it LOW along the floor like something running away, and say TAKE IT.
steps.look: She grabs it. If she is already leaping and snatching before the game starts, put it away and try after her next nap.

steps.do: Keep it low and side to side. Never up in the air, never lifting her front feet off the ground, never shaking her.
steps.look: Her feet stay down. She is ten weeks old, those are milk teeth, and her neck, shoulders and growth plates are years from finished.

steps.do: Every 15 or 20 seconds, freeze. Go completely still and boring, hold the toy dead, and say DROP once.
steps.look: She lets go. Marker, food, and then TAKE IT again straight away. Restarting the game is the real payment, and it is why the drop stays reliable instead of decaying.

steps.do: You end it while she still wants more. Toy goes away, out of her reach, out of sight.
steps.look: She is still keen when it disappears. That is what you want, every time.

steps.do: Teeth on skin ends the game instantly. No telling off, no noise. Stand up, toy behind your back, ten seconds, then try again.
steps.look: She learns that her aim is what keeps the game running.

steps.do: The suction cup toy, and what is wrong with the box. It is sold as self-play and while-you-are-out. Do not use it that way. Stick it down, sit next to it, keep a hand on the rope, and play exactly the game above.
steps.look: Two reasons, and both are real. A floor anchor has no give, so she pulls against her own body weight with milk teeth and there is nobody there to freeze and cue DROP. And it is rope: swallowed strands are a linear foreign body, which is worse than swallowing a solid object and is a surgical emergency.

steps.do: Check the rope every single time, before and after. Then put it away.
steps.look: Fraying, a loose strand, a chewed-through section, a suction base she has started working at: bin it. Nothing is indestructible and the listing that says so is selling something.

wrong: Letting her end the game by snatching it and running off. Who ends it is the difference between a rule and a scuffle.
Lifting her off the floor, swinging her, or letting her hang. Not at any age, and absolutely not at ten weeks.
Growling and wrestling back. Keep it light and keep it a game.
Leaving any tug toy on the floor. Tug is a game with a person in it. A tug toy without you is just a rope she can eat.
Playing tug with an overtired puppy. If she cannot hear DROP, she needed a nap twenty minutes ago.
skills.note: The one thing about this toy that is genuinely good: it lets you play tug one-handed, or with the rope anchored while you cue her from a step away, which is a nice way to build a drop at distance later. The one thing about it that is genuinely bad is everything the listing promises. Use it as a toy you supervise and it is fine.

criteria.test: TAKE IT starts the game, with the toy low on the floor.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: You freeze and say DROP once, no food visible.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: She is fully into it and you cue DROP once.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: A full 90 second game.
criteria.pass: No contact at all, 4 sessions out of 5.

criteria.test: You end it and put the toy away while she still wants more.
criteria.pass: She settles within a minute rather than barking at you, 4 out of 5.

skills.title: Ringing to ask to go out
skills.age: Start now. It will not pay off until about four months, and that is normal.
skills.sessions: Ten seconds at every potty trip. Never a session of its own.
skills.why: It gives her one clear way to tell you, instead of pacing, circling and whining, which three different people will read three different ways. Be honest about what it is not: it does not house-train her. The clock and the schedule do that. What the bell buys you is everything from about four months onward, when she can actually hold it and needs a way to say so.
need: ONE bell. Not both of them.
The one door she always goes out of for potty
Her kibble for the first week or so, then nothing

steps.do: Pick one device and put the other in a cupboard. Use the wireless button: mount it by the potty door at her nose height, on the LOWEST volume.
steps.look: The doorknob bells jingle on their own every time anybody opens or shuts that door, which is a false alarm several times a day and teaches her the sound means nothing. The button only makes a noise when she touches it, and the chime carries to another room, which matters when three people share her and one of you is on a Zoom shiur. Keep the doorknob bells as the spare, or for a house where there is nowhere to mount a button.

steps.do: Charge it as a target first, in your hand, off the wall, volume at its lowest. Hold it out flat. The instant her nose touches it: marker, food.
steps.look: Nose, not paw. Pay the nose and ignore the paw and you will get a nose for life. A hundred and fifteen decibels six inches from a ten week old puppy's face is how you get a puppy who is frightened of the door, so start quiet and turn it up over a fortnight.
steps.reps: 6 to 8, twice a day, for two days.

steps.do: Mount it low by the door. At the START of every single potty trip, point at it. She touches it, marker, food, and you open the door immediately.
steps.look: The door opening becomes the real reward. Fade the food out over about a week and let the door do the paying.
steps.reps: Every trip. All three of you, every time.

steps.do: Stop pointing. Stand at the door with the leash and wait three to five seconds, saying nothing.
steps.look: She touches it on her own. If she does not, point once, pay, and make the next one easier. Never stand there repeating a cue at her.

steps.do: Out on the leash, straight to the potty spot, and be boring. No walk, no sniffing tour, no saying hello to anyone. She goes, you pay her out there at the spot, and you come back in.
steps.look: This step, and only this step, decides whether the bell comes to mean 'I need to pee' or 'I want to go outside'. What is on the other side of the door is the whole lesson.

steps.do: From around four months, when she can genuinely hold it: any unprompted touch gets answered. Every time, however inconvenient, for the first month.
steps.look: A bell that works only sometimes is a bell she stops using. After that first month, if she is ringing constantly, read the bell entry in the Guide.

wrong: Running both the doorknob bells and the button. Two signals for one need, and she learns neither.
Also teaching an OUTSIDE button on the soundboard. That is the same mistake a third time.
Full volume on her first press. Start at the lowest setting.

Treating it as house training. It is not. She is about ten weeks, she can hold roughly two and a half hours awake, and she does not yet feel it coming in advance. Until four months or so this is you building a habit she will use later.
Ringing it for her over and over hoping she copies you. She will learn that the noise happens near the door and nothing more. Shape the nose touch.
Playing outside straight after a bell trip. That is how you buy yourself a dog who rings it forty times a day.
skills.note: Two bells arrived for one job. Pick the button, and do not feel bad about the other one costing eight dollars: running both is worse than owning one. The doorknob bells are the better choice in exactly one situation, which is somewhere you cannot fix a button to the wall, so keep them in the trip bag.

criteria.test: The button held out flat in your hand, off the wall.
criteria.pass: Nose touch, 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: Mounted by the door, you point once at the start of a trip.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 trips across a day.

criteria.test: You stand at the door with the leash and wait five seconds.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 trips.

criteria.test: She goes to the door and touches it without you being there first.
criteria.pass: Three separate times in a week. Expect this from about four months, not before.

criteria.test: She rings, you take her straight out, and she actually eliminates.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 rings over two weeks. Below that, read the bell entry in the Guide.

skills.title: Clean paws at the door
skills.age: Now, while she is small and everything is a game.
skills.sessions: 1 to 2 minutes, at every return home.
skills.why: You asked for this one specifically. It is worth doing properly, because paw handling is one of the most common things adult dogs hate, and every future nail trim depends on it. Done right at 10 weeks, it takes a fortnight. Done at a year old, after she has learned to pull her feet away, it takes months.
need: A damp cloth or a paw mat by the door
Kibble in a pot by the door, refilled daily
One consistent word: CLEAN

steps.do: Away from the door, with no cloth in sight. Touch one paw for one second. Say YES, feed. That is it.
steps.look: She lets you touch it without pulling away. If she pulls back, touch her leg above the paw instead and work down over a few days.
steps.reps: 8 touches, spread over the day. All four paws.

steps.do: Hold the paw for two seconds, then three, then five. Mark and pay while you are still holding it, not after you let go.
steps.look: Marking after you release teaches her that pulling away ends it. Mark DURING the hold.

steps.do: Introduce the cloth as an object. Let her sniff it, pay her for sniffing it. Do not touch her with it yet.
steps.look: The cloth predicts food before it ever predicts handling.

steps.do: Touch the cloth to one paw for one second. YES, feed. Build up: one wipe, then two, then all four paws.
steps.look: She stands still. If she pulls a foot away, that wipe was a second too long. Shorten it.

steps.do: Add the word CLEAN as you start, once she is comfortable. Same word from all three of you.
steps.look: She offers the paw or stands still when she hears it.

steps.do: Do it at the door, in the real routine, with her leash still on.
steps.look: She comes in, stops on the mat, and waits.

wrong: Doing all four paws on day one because you need to. If she is muddy and untrained, just wipe her and accept it is not a training rep. Do the training reps separately, when nothing needs cleaning.
Holding on when she pulls. She has to learn that stillness ends it, not struggle. Let go at a calm moment, not a struggling one.
Only touching her paws when they need cleaning. Then paw touching predicts something she does not want.
skills.note: The same protocol builds toward nail trims. Once she is happy with paw holding, start touching her nails with the clippers without cutting, paying every time, for a couple of weeks before you ever cut one.

criteria.test: You can hold each of her four paws for five seconds, away from the door, with no cloth.
criteria.pass: All four paws, no pulling away, 5 out of 6 attempts.

criteria.test: You can wipe all four paws with a damp cloth.
criteria.pass: All four, no wriggling, twice in a row on different days.

criteria.test: You say CLEAN at the door and she stops and stands.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 returns home.

criteria.test: She goes to the mat and waits when you come in, without a cue.
criteria.pass: Happens by itself on 8 out of 10 returns.

criteria.test: All three of you can do it, and she is equally relaxed for a vet or groomer holding her paw.
criteria.pass: Each handler can do all four paws.

skills.title: Being handled all over
skills.age: Now. This has a deadline.
skills.why: Her socialization window closes around 12 to 16 weeks. What she learns to accept now, she accepts for life; what she first meets at eight months, she can find genuinely frightening. Every vet visit, every ear clean, every tick check, every emergency for the next twelve years runs on this. It is the least glamorous skill on the list and probably the highest value.
need: Kibble
Two minutes
A calm moment, not after play

steps.do: Sit next to her when she is settled. Touch one ear for one second. YES, feed.
steps.look: She does not move away.

steps.do: Work through the map, one area per session: ears, then around the eyes, then muzzle, then lift a lip to see the teeth, then paws, then between the toes, then tail, then belly, then the collar.
steps.look: Each one gets its own days. Do not rush through the map in one sitting.

steps.do: Build duration. One second becomes three, becomes five. Mark and feed DURING, not after.
steps.look: She stays relaxed. Loose body, no lip licking, no whale eye, not turning her head away.

steps.do: Add the things a vet does: hold her still with a hand on her chest and her rear. Look in her ears. Run your hands down each leg. Lift her.
steps.look: None of it is novel by the time a vet does it.

steps.do: Have Shira and Chayim do it too, on separate days. Then do it in a different room, on a table, on a towel.
steps.look: She accepts handling from people who are not you, which is the actual test.

wrong: Waiting until something needs doing. The first ear clean should not be the first time anyone has touched her ears.
Pushing past her discomfort to finish. If she pulls away, you went one second too long. Shorten it, do not force it.
Restraining her tightly. The goal is a puppy who chooses to stay still, not one who has learned struggling is pointless.
skills.note: Take kibble to the vet tomorrow and pay her on the table, in the waiting room, and on the scales, whether or not anything happens. A vet visit that involves food is a different memory from one that does not.

criteria.test: You can touch every area on the map for one second each.
criteria.pass: All areas, no avoidance, in one session.

criteria.test: Five-second holds on ears, muzzle, paws, belly, tail.
criteria.pass: All five, loose body, twice on different days.

criteria.test: A full mock exam: restrain, ears, eyes, teeth, all four legs, belly, lift.
criteria.pass: Whole sequence, no struggling, twice.

criteria.test: All three handlers can do the mock exam.
criteria.pass: Each handler, once.

criteria.test: A mock exam somewhere unfamiliar, on a table or a towel.
criteria.pass: Whole sequence, calm, once.

skills.title: The play gym, and confidence with new things
skills.age: Now, and it has a deadline: the confidence half closes with the socialization window at 16 weeks.
skills.sessions: 3 to 5 minutes, once a day, with you in the room. It counts as play, not as training.
skills.why: Two things it is genuinely good for, and one it is not. It is a novel object: something new-shaped, wobbly and noisy standing in the middle of the living room, and a puppy who learns to walk up to strange things and investigate is doing socialization work against a real deadline. And its hanging toys give her somewhere legal to put her mouth. What it is NOT is agility equipment, whatever the listing says. She is a large-breed puppy and repetitive jumping is the one thing she must not do.
need: The frame, standing on carpet or a rug, never on tile or wood
Kibble from the day's container
You, in the room, the whole time it is out

steps.do: Build it, stand it where she lives, and then ignore it completely for a day. Scatter three pieces of kibble a foot away from it, not underneath.
steps.look: She walks past it without giving it a wide berth. If she is worried by it, more distance and better food, never a nudge toward it.

steps.do: Pay her for noticing it. Every glance at it: marker, food, delivered away from the frame.
steps.look: She starts looking at it deliberately to make you pay. That is exactly right.

steps.do: Pay a step toward it, then a nose on it, then a paw on the base.
steps.look: Each rung is her choice. She approaches; you never carry her to it.
steps.reps: 6 to 8, over two or three days.

steps.do: Feed her under and through it. Kibble on the floor inside the frame so she has to put her head and shoulders under the bar.
steps.look: Head under, body relaxed, tail loose. That is the confidence repetition and it is the whole point of the thing.

steps.do: Now the hanging toys. Take one, hold it steady, wiggle it, let her tug it for ten seconds and cue DROP. The tug rules apply here in full.
steps.look: She engages the toy, not the frame, and lets go on the cue.

steps.do: Harder, and this is the only harder that is safe: MOVE it. A different room, a different floor, next to something noisy, with different toys clipped on. Not higher. Never a jump.
steps.look: She approaches it the same way somewhere she has never seen it.

steps.do: Retire it when she outgrows it, which will be soon. It is a 17 inch cube built for small dogs and rated to about six months.
steps.look: Her back level with the top bar, or her able to drag the whole frame, means it is done. She is heading for about 65 pounds. Do not replace it with a bigger one; put the money into a class.

wrong: Using it as a jump, or as something to climb on and off. Her growth plates are open and stay open until roughly 12 to 18 months in a large breed. Repeated impact through an open growth plate shows up as a joint problem years later, not on the day.
Leaving her alone with it. It is a wooden frame with rope and squeaky toys hanging off it, which is precisely the list of things that must never be in front of her unsupervised.
Standing it on wood or tile. She slips, it slides, and what she learns is that the thing is dangerous.
Lifting her onto it or pushing her under it. Every rung here has to be her choosing to move toward it.
Reading it as exercise. It is a thinking toy that happens to be a climbing frame shape. Her exercise limit is five minutes of walk per month of age, twice a day, and this does not change that.
skills.note: Every time she chooses to walk up to a new thing on her own and gets paid for it, you are buying an adult dog who is not frightened of the vet's scale, a folded umbrella, or a steel plate on the sidewalk. That is what this frame is actually for, and the frame itself is disposable. Of the seven things you bought, this is the one with the shortest useful life.

criteria.test: It stands in the room where she lives.
criteria.pass: She walks past it without a wide berth or a startle.

criteria.test: You wait and pay her for moving toward it.
criteria.pass: She goes to it on her own, 5 out of 6 offers.

criteria.test: Kibble on the floor inside the frame.
criteria.pass: She puts her head under the bar with a loose body, 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: A hanging toy, you holding it steady.
criteria.pass: She tugs, and lets go on one DROP, 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: The frame moved to a different room or a different floor.
criteria.pass: Same approach and same head-under, first time, 4 out of 5.

skills.title: Learning to accept a bath
skills.age: Now. This one has a deadline.
skills.sessions: 2 to 5 minutes, twice a day at most. Never right after a walk when she is tired.
skills.why: Bath fear is a learning problem, not a compliance problem. Every bath she is held through teaches her one thing: struggling does not work, and the people I trust will hold me down. What you get from forcing it is not a calm dog, it is a dog who has learned helplessness, which looks like calm right up until the day the restraint is not enough. Then you have a 70 lb dog with a decade of practised fear. Her socialisation window closes around 16 weeks, so you have roughly six weeks of the cheapest learning she will ever do. Ten short sessions over three weeks now costs less than a behaviour consult and years of sedated grooming later.
need: A non-slip mat for the tub, used from the very first session even when the tub is dry
A suction lickmat
Genuinely high value food: wet food, plain cooked chicken, cream cheese. Kibble will not carry this.
Nothing else. No water for the first three steps.

steps.do: The room. Door open, tub dry and empty. Feed her a meal on the bathroom floor.
steps.look: She walks into the bathroom on her own and eats normally.
steps.reps: One meal a day for a few days.

steps.do: The dry tub. Non-slip mat down. Lure her in with food, or lift her in and feed immediately, then lift out after five seconds.
steps.look: She steps in voluntarily, or is lifted in without stiffening, and eats in the tub.

steps.do: Sound. She is in the dry tub on the lickmat. Turn the tap on for three seconds, then off. Food continues three seconds longer, then stops.
steps.look: She keeps licking through the tap noise. Best case she looks at the tap and then at you, which means the association is forming.

steps.do: One wet paw. Damp washcloth on one front paw. Food. Remove the cloth and the food stops.
steps.look: She eats through it. No pulling the paw away, no freezing.

steps.do: Water on the body, no shampoo. Warm water on her hind feet and legs only, ten seconds. Towel. Done. Nothing else happens.
steps.look: She stays standing, keeps eating, does not try to climb out.

steps.do: Half a dog. Wet her from the shoulders back. Towel. Out. Still no shampoo.
steps.look: Same as above, tolerating about sixty seconds of water.

steps.do: Add shampoo, still not a full bath. Whole body wet, dilute shampoo on the back only, quick rinse, out. Skip the head, skip the feathering, skip anything difficult.
steps.look: The whole thing under five minutes and she is still eating.

steps.do: The real bath, the full sequence.
steps.look: She completes it without struggling.

criteria.test: She walks into the bathroom on her own and eats a meal on the floor.
criteria.pass: Two sessions running, with two different handlers.

criteria.test: She is in the tub on the mat, eating.
criteria.pass: Two sessions running, two handlers.

criteria.test: Tap on for three seconds while she is on the lickmat.
criteria.pass: She keeps licking through it, 4 out of 5 reps.

criteria.test: Warm water on her hind legs for ten seconds.
criteria.pass: Still eating, not trying to leave, twice on different days.

criteria.test: The full sequence from the guide.
criteria.pass: Completed without struggle, twice.

wrong: Pushing through when she has stopped eating. Refusing food is the single most reliable sign she is over threshold. If she stops eating, you went too far: back up one step.

Finishing the job. For the next four to six baths, deliberately STOP BEFORE SHE IS CLEAN. Wet her, do one section, dry, release. A half-done bath that ends well teaches that baths are short and survivable. A complete bath that ends badly teaches that once she is in there it never ends. You are training the dog, not cleaning her.

Two people where the second one holds her. That is restraint with extra staff, and it teaches her that two humans are now part of the bad thing. The second person feeds and talks and never restrains. If she wants to leave, she may leave.
Skipping the non-slip mat at step 2 because the tub is dry. Footing is a primary fear variable, not a nicety.
One handler quietly just getting it done. That resets the other two by weeks. All three of you run the same step.
skills.note: Timeline: if she is only mildly worried, steps 1 to 8 take two to three weeks. If she is genuinely frightened, budget six to eight weeks and split the steps further. There is no prize for finishing fast, and she does not need a real bath in the meantime because she is clean. If after about three weeks of consistent work she still panics at step 3 or 4, that is past a self-help protocol: ask your vet for a referral to a veterinary behaviourist. At 10 weeks that is a short cheap intervention. At 10 months it is not.

skills.title: Loving the crate
skills.age: Now, and it should never have been rushed.
skills.why: The crate has to be the best place in the apartment, not the place she goes when everyone is done with her. A puppy who chooses to go in on her own is safe to leave; a puppy who is put in is a puppy who is learning to dread it. This is also the foundation of being left alone, which is a separate skill she genuinely has to be taught.
need: Her crate, divider set so she can stand, turn and lie down and no more
A stuffed frozen Kong from her ration
Her bed

steps.do: Door propped fully open, all day. Drop a piece of kibble in it every time you walk past and she is not looking.
steps.look: She starts checking it herself. Say nothing. Do not lure her in, do not praise her for going in. Let it be her discovery.

steps.do: Feed her meals in it, door still open. Start with the bowl just inside, then further back over a few days.
steps.look: She goes in willingly to eat.

steps.do: Give her the frozen Kong in there, door open. Let her come out whenever she likes.
steps.look: She settles in there by choice.

steps.do: Close the door for five seconds while she has the Kong. Open it before she finishes. Build to thirty seconds, a minute, five minutes.
steps.look: Open the door BEFORE she wants out, every time. If you wait until she asks, you have taught her that asking works.

steps.do: Close the door and move around the room. Then step out of sight for a moment. Then longer.
steps.look: She stays settled. Any whining means your last step was too big. Go back two steps.

steps.do: Add a word: BED or CRATE, said as she goes in, once she is going in reliably by herself.
steps.look: She goes in on the word, for a Kong.

wrong: Putting her in and shutting the door on day one. That is the single fastest way to build a dog who panics in a crate.
Letting her out while she is crying. That pays the crying. Wait for two seconds of quiet, then open. If she is crying a lot, the steps were too big, not her fault.
Using the crate as punishment. Ever.
A crate that is too big. A puppy will use one end as a toilet if she has room to move away from it.

criteria.test: She goes in on her own during the day, unprompted.
criteria.pass: You see it happen several times a day without you doing anything.

criteria.test: She eats a full meal inside with the door open.
criteria.pass: Every meal for three days.

criteria.test: Door shut for five minutes with a Kong while you are in the room.
criteria.pass: Settled, no whining, three times.

criteria.test: Door shut, you out of sight for ten minutes.
criteria.pass: Settled, twice on different days.

criteria.test: You say the word, she goes in, and she settles without a Kong.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6, and she sleeps in there overnight without distress.

skills.title: Switching off
skills.age: Now. She probably needs this more than she needs sit.
skills.why: A 10 week old puppy needs somewhere between 18 and 20 hours of sleep a day, and most puppy problems people describe as naughtiness are actually overtiredness. Biting, zoomies, ignoring cues, frantic chewing. A puppy who cannot switch off does not learn to; it is a skill, and you can teach it, mostly by paying it when it happens by accident.
need: A mat or bed in the room you use most
Kibble
Patience, and the willingness to do nothing

steps.do: Put the mat down. Sit near it and read something. Say nothing. Ignore her.
steps.look: Eventually she gets bored and lies down. The instant she does, calmly drop a piece of kibble between her paws. Do not say YES, do not make a fuss. Quiet reward for quiet behavior.

steps.do: Keep dropping food, slowly, while she stays down. One piece every few seconds, then every ten, then every thirty.
steps.look: She stays. You are paying duration, not the act of lying down.

steps.do: Any time during the day that you notice her settled on her own, walk over and quietly drop a piece of food. Then walk away.
steps.look: Settling starts happening more often, because it has been paid.
steps.reps: Whenever you notice. This is the whole skill.

steps.do: Add the word SETTLE, said quietly as she is already lying down, once it is happening reliably.
steps.look: Later, the word starts to prompt it.

steps.do: Practice in more stimulating places: near the door, with the TV on, in the kitchen while you cook.
steps.look: She can switch off with things happening.

wrong: Excited praise when she settles. That wakes her up and undoes it. Quiet, boring reward only.
Assuming she will settle when she is overtired. An overtired puppy cannot. She needs the crate and a nap, not a training session.
Only trying it when she is wild. Start when she is already sleepy and you are paying something that was going to happen anyway.
skills.note: If she is biting hard, racing around, and cannot take food, she is almost certainly overtired rather than badly behaved. Crate, dark, quiet, and try again in an hour.

criteria.test: She lies down on the mat within five minutes of you sitting quietly with it.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4 attempts.

criteria.test: She stays settled for five minutes with occasional quiet food.
criteria.pass: Twice on different days.

criteria.test: She holds a settle for ten minutes with only two or three pieces of food.
criteria.pass: Twice.

criteria.test: You say SETTLE and she goes to the mat and lies down.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: She settles while you cook, or while someone is at the door.
criteria.pass: Ten minutes, twice, in two different situations.

skills.title: The food puzzle
skills.age: Now. Level 1 at one meal today.
skills.sessions: One meal a day through it, about 10 minutes. This is not a training session and it does not come out of the 15 minutes. It replaces a bowl.
skills.why: Sniffing and problem-solving tire a puppy in a way walking does not, which matters enormously for a large-breed puppy who must not be exercised hard. It slows her eating down. And it is what you use when a walk is not happening: rain, a storm, the Monday shiur, a Shabbat afternoon. It costs nothing, because it IS her meal, not an extra.
need: The puzzle, on a rug or a towel so it cannot slide
Her measured kibble, out of the day's one container
A spot where nobody has to step over her

steps.do: Before she ever sees it work: stand it on the floor and scatter ten pieces of kibble AROUND it, none inside. Let her eat off the floor next to it and walk away.
steps.look: She eats near it without backing off from it. That is the whole first day.

steps.do: Level 1, made free. Every opening wide open, and half the food sitting on top in plain sight where she can just take it.
steps.look: She gets food within about three seconds of putting her nose on it. The first experience has to be almost free or she quits, and a puppy who has quit on a puzzle once is hard to get back.

steps.do: Level 1 properly. Food inside the open wells only, nothing on top.
steps.look: She noses and paws at it and keeps working for two or three minutes without walking off.
steps.reps: Once a day for about a week.

steps.do: Level 2, and only when she empties level 1 in under two minutes on three days running. If she stalls, go back to level 1 for a week. There is no prize for getting through the levels fast.
steps.look: She works at it. Barking at it or flipping it means it is too hard.

steps.do: Level 3, same rule again. Three easy days at level 2 first.
steps.look: Steady work, no giving up, no smashing.

steps.do: Once level 3 is easy, make it harder the OTHER way: same puzzle, new room, on carpet instead of tile, with you further away, or with something mildly distracting going on.
steps.look: She still settles into it somewhere unfamiliar.

steps.do: Rotate. Two or three different food toys taking turns beats one puzzle every single day, which stops being work and becomes a routine.
steps.look: She still gets interested when it comes out.

wrong: Starting at level 3 because she seems clever. The first go has to be nearly free. Frustration at a food toy is the one failure that makes her worse at the next one.

Helping her. Do not dig the food out for her. If she has not solved it in about five minutes, take it up without a word and make it easier tomorrow. Helping teaches her to look at you when a thing gets hard, which is the opposite of what the toy is for.
Leaving it down when it is empty. It becomes a chew toy, and it has a squeaker in it. See the crate toys entry in the Guide.
Reaching in or hovering over her while she works. That is how you build a dog who guards a food toy.
Adding food for it. Everything in there came out of the day's container, so the bowl gets less that day. It is not an extra meal.
skills.note: The listing calls it levels 1 to 3 and that is a genuine progression, so use it: it means you do not have to guess how hard to make it. But the level is only one of the two dials. The other is where she does it and what else is going on, and that dial is the one that transfers to real life.

criteria.test: Level 1 with every opening wide and half the food on top.
criteria.pass: She works it for two minutes without walking away, 3 sessions running.

criteria.test: Food inside the open wells only.
criteria.pass: She empties it, 4 sessions out of 5.

criteria.test: The next difficulty setting.
criteria.pass: She empties it inside three minutes, 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: The hardest setting.
criteria.pass: She empties it inside three minutes, 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: A puzzle she cannot solve straight away, somewhere unfamiliar.
criteria.pass: She keeps working for a full minute without barking at it, biting it or walking off. 4 out of 5.

skills.title: Bite inhibition
skills.age: Now. This has a hard deadline of about 18 weeks.
skills.why: This is not about stopping her biting. It is about teaching her HOW HARD is too hard, while her jaw is still too weak to do damage. A dog who has learned that teeth on skin means the game stops has a soft mouth for life, and if she is ever frightened or in pain at eight years old, that learning is what stands between a snap and a serious bite. You cannot teach this later; the window is now.
need: Nothing. Just consistency between all three of you.
Two or three chew toys within reach in every room.

steps.do: Play with her using your hands. When teeth make contact hard enough to be uncomfortable, stop immediately. Stand up, fold your arms, turn away, and be completely boring for 10 to 20 seconds.
steps.look: The game stops the instant it hurts. That is the entire lesson: teeth end fun.

steps.do: After 10 to 20 seconds, calmly resume. Do not scold, do not make a scene, do not leave the room for minutes.
steps.look: Short and immediate beats long and delayed. She needs the consequence connected to the bite, not to whatever she did next.

steps.do: Lower the bar over the weeks. First stop only for hard bites. Then for medium ones. Then for any tooth contact at all.
steps.look: She graduates from no hard bites to no teeth on skin. By about 18 weeks you want zero tooth contact.

steps.do: Redirect. Before the bite, not after: have a toy in your other hand and put it where your fingers were.
steps.look: She learns what teeth ARE for. A puppy with nothing to bite will bite you.

steps.do: Check the clock. If it has been more than an hour since she slept and the biting is frantic, that is not a training moment.
steps.look: Overtired biting does not respond to training because she cannot think. Crate, quiet, nap.

wrong: Yelping loudly. This one is genuinely contested. Dunbar's protocol uses it, but the AKC, the ASPCA and Whole Dog Journal all independently report that a high-pitched yelp winds many puppies UP rather than calming them, because it sounds like prey. If yelping makes her bite harder, stop yelping and just go quiet and still.

Muzzle-holding, scruffing, alpha rolls, or pinning her. Herron 2009 measured the outcomes: growling at the dog provoked aggression in 41 percent, an alpha roll in 31 percent, muzzle grabs in 26 percent. These make it worse and they make her afraid of hands.
Pulling your hand away fast. That triggers the chase and grab reflex. Go still instead.
Punishing her for biting without giving her anything legal to bite. She is teething and she has to chew something.
skills.note: She will bite for weeks. That is developmentally normal and it is not aggression. What matters is the trend: is it getting softer and less frequent over a fortnight. If it is not, or if it comes with growling, stiffening or guarding, get a qualified behaviorist involved rather than escalating.

criteria.test: A ten minute play session with your hands.
criteria.pass: No bite hard enough to make you flinch. Three sessions running.

criteria.test: Same, judging medium pressure.
criteria.pass: No medium bites in three sessions.

criteria.test: She takes the toy when you offer it instead of your hand.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 offers.

criteria.test: Play, stroking, and handling with no tooth contact on skin at all.
criteria.pass: Three consecutive days, across all three handlers.

criteria.test: No tooth contact even during exciting play or when guests arrive.
criteria.pass: Consistently, by around 18 weeks.

skills.title: Down
skills.age: From about 12 weeks, once sit is at Named.
skills.why: Down is harder than sit, because lying down is a vulnerable position and a puppy has to feel safe to offer it. It is also the foundation of settle, of stay, and of a dog who can be taken to a cafe.
need: Kibble
A soft, non-slip surface. A rug, not a wooden floor.

steps.do: Start with her in a sit. Hold food at her nose and lower it straight down to the floor between her front paws, then slide it slowly toward you along the ground.
steps.look: Her elbows drop as she follows it. Mark the instant her elbows touch. If her bottom comes up, you moved too fast or too far forward.

steps.do: If she will not follow it down, sit on the floor with one knee up and lure her under your knee.
steps.look: She has to duck to get the food, which puts her down.

steps.do: Same motion, empty hand. Reward from the other hand.
steps.look: She follows the empty gesture.

steps.do: Shrink the gesture to a small downward point.
steps.look: She goes down off a small signal.

steps.do: Add the word DOWN once, then the gesture.
steps.look: She beats the gesture within a few sessions.

wrong: Using DOWN to also mean get off the sofa and stop jumping. Three meanings, one word, no learning. Pick OFF for those.
Pushing her shoulders down.
Trying it on a slippery floor where she cannot get purchase.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: Somewhere she has never done it before. Treats in a pocket or a closed pouch, not in your hand. One cue, no repeats.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 first-time responses. THIS is the answer to did she learn it. Not once. Not sometimes. Eight out of ten, cold, in a new place.

skills.title: Wait and stay
skills.age: From 12 weeks.
skills.why: Stay is really three separate skills that people try to train as one, which is why it usually falls apart: duration, distance, and distraction. Train them one at a time and never two at once. Every time you raise one, drop the other two.
need: Kibble
A release word, decided now and written down. OK or FREE or BREAK.

steps.do: Teach the release word first. Put her in a sit, immediately say OK and encourage her to move, then reward the movement.
steps.look: She understands there is a word that means you are finished. Without it, stay has no end and she decides when it ends.

steps.do: DURATION only. Sit, count one second, mark, feed, then release. Then two seconds. Then three. Stay right next to her.
steps.look: Build in ones and twos. If she breaks, your last increment was too big.
steps.reps: 6 per session, varying the count so it is not always increasing.

steps.do: DISTANCE only. Go back to one second, but take half a step back. Then a full step. Then two.
steps.look: Return TO HER to reward. If you call her to you, you are rewarding coming, not staying.

steps.do: DISTRACTION only. Back to one second, right next to her, but now bounce a ball, or have someone walk past.
steps.look: She holds. Start with distractions so mild they barely register.

steps.do: Combine slowly, two at a time, always dropping the third right down.
steps.look: Three seconds at three steps with someone walking past is a hard problem. Get there in months, not days.

steps.do: Add WAIT for the short version at doors and curbs, and STAY for the long one, if you want two words. Or use one for both.
steps.look: Consistent across all three of you.

wrong: Raising duration, distance and distraction at once. This is why most stays fail.
Calling her out of a stay. Always go back to her.
Repeating STAY as a nervous tic while she is holding it. Say it once and be quiet.
No release word, so she decides when it is over.

criteria.test: She moves on OK and not before.
criteria.pass: 6 out of 6.

criteria.test: 30 seconds, you standing next to her, no distractions.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4 attempts.

criteria.test: 10 seconds while you stand three meters away.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4.

criteria.test: 10 seconds, next to her, with a toy bounced in front of her.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4.

criteria.test: 30 seconds, five meters away, in a room with something going on.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4, and it holds in two different rooms.

skills.title: Loose lead walking
skills.age: From 12 weeks. Expect this to take months, not weeks.
skills.sessions: 5 minutes, and separately from actual walks.
skills.why: The hardest thing on this list, and the one people rush. Pulling is self-rewarding: she pulls, she gets closer to the smell, pulling works. Until walking next to you pays better than pulling does, she will pull. Do her toilet trips and her exercise as normal, and train this as its own separate exercise.
need: A flat collar or a Y-shaped harness. Never a choke, prong or slip leash on a growing puppy.
A 6 foot leash. Never retractable.
Chicken, not kibble, to start.

steps.do: Indoors, no leash at all. Walk a few steps. Every time she is next to your leg, mark and feed AT YOUR LEG, at her head height.
steps.look: She starts to hang around your left side because that is where food appears.

steps.do: Add the leash, still indoors. Same game. The leash should hang in a J shape and never go tight.
steps.look: She ignores the leash entirely.

steps.do: Hallway, then just outside the door. Pay far more often than feels reasonable. Every two or three steps at first.
steps.look: Outside is a hundred times harder than inside. Your payment rate has to go up accordingly.

steps.do: THE RULE: the leash going tight means all forward motion stops. Stand still. Say nothing. Wait.
steps.look: When the leash slackens, even by accident, mark and move off. She learns pulling stops the walk and slack starts it.
steps.reps: Every single time, from every handler.

steps.do: Give her sniffing time on cue. Say GO SNIFF and let her have three minutes on a loose leash to do whatever she likes.
steps.look: Sniffing is the point of the walk for her. If the whole walk is heelwork she has no reason to cooperate. Trade structured walking for sniffing time.

wrong: Training this on a walk where you actually need to get somewhere. You will give in and let her pull, and that pays the pulling. Separate the two.
Jerking the leash. It does not teach position, it teaches that being next to you sometimes hurts.
A retractable leash. It teaches her that constant tension is normal, which is the exact opposite of the lesson.
Expecting a formal heel. You want a loose leash, not a dog glued to your knee. Those are different skills and only one of them is useful.
skills.note: Her exercise limit still applies. Structured leash walking counts toward it. Free sniffing and pottering does not count the same way. Keep the total in line with her age.

criteria.test: Ten steps with the leash loose, indoors.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4 attempts.

criteria.test: Twenty steps outside your front door with a loose leash.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4.

criteria.test: Fifty meters on a quiet sidewalk without the leash going tight.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4 outings.

criteria.test: Two minutes of continuous loose-leash walking on a normal street.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4 outings.

criteria.test: A whole ten minute walk where the leash is loose more than it is tight, past other people and dogs.
criteria.pass: Consistently over a fortnight.

skills.title: Waiting at doors
skills.age: From 12 weeks.
skills.sessions: Every time you go through a door.
skills.why: A door-darting puppy in a city flat is a genuine safety problem. This also becomes your curb behavior, which matters more every month.
need: Kibble
Any door

steps.do: Hand on the door handle. If she surges, take your hand off. Say nothing.
steps.look: She learns her movement controls the door, not yours.

steps.do: Open the door an inch. If she moves forward, close it. If she holds still, mark and feed.
steps.look: Stillness opens the door.

steps.do: Build to fully open with her holding position.
steps.look: She waits at an open door.

steps.do: Release her through with OK. Reward on the other side sometimes, and sometimes call her back and reward for that instead.
steps.look: She does not assume an open door is an invitation.

steps.do: Take it to the curb. Stop at every curb, ask for a sit, then release.
steps.look: An automatic curb stop by about six months.

wrong: Only doing it when you remember. Doors are all-or-nothing; inconsistency here teaches her to try her luck.
Letting a visitor open the door without knowing the rule.

criteria.test: You touch the handle and she does not surge.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: Door open a few inches, she holds.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: Door fully open, she holds for five seconds.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: The same at your actual front door, with the hall beyond.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: She stops at doors and curbs without being asked.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 occasions, with all three handlers.

skills.title: Being left alone
skills.age: Now, in tiny doses. It is genuinely urgent.
skills.sessions: Several very short absences a day.
skills.why: Being alone is not natural to a dog and it is not something she grows into. It has to be taught, deliberately, in seconds before minutes. The single biggest predictor of separation problems is never having practised it while things were calm. She has three people around constantly at the moment, which makes this easy to forget and expensive to skip.
need: Her crate or a pen, already a good place
A stuffed frozen Kong from her ration
A phone camera or old tablet to watch her

steps.do: With her settled in the crate with a Kong, walk to the other side of the room. Come back before she looks up.
steps.look: She does not notice you left.

steps.do: Step out of the room for two seconds. Return calmly. No greeting, no fuss.
steps.look: Coming and going is unremarkable.

steps.do: Build the time in an irregular pattern: 5 seconds, 20, 10, 45, 15, 2. Never a steady climb.
steps.look: She cannot predict how long it will be, so she does not start counting.

steps.do: Once you are past a minute, do the full leaving routine: shoes, keys, coat, door. Then come straight back in.
steps.look: The departure cues stop predicting a long absence.

steps.do: Actually leave the apartment. Two minutes. Five. Ten. Watch her on camera.
steps.look: Settled or asleep. If she is pacing, whining, drooling or scratching, you went too fast. Go back to a duration she was fine with.

wrong: Big emotional goodbyes and big greetings. Both make your absence the most significant event of her day. Be boring at both ends.
Only practising when you have to go out. Then leaving always means a long absence.
Assuming a quiet puppy is a settled puppy. Watch the camera. Silent pacing and drooling is distress.
Pushing through distress hoping she will get used to it. She will not; she will get worse. Distress is the signal to go back a step.
skills.note: Genuine separation anxiety is a clinical condition, not a training failure, and it responds much better to early help. If she is panicking rather than just protesting, that is a conversation for your vet.

criteria.test: Two minutes alone in a room while you are elsewhere in the apartment.
criteria.pass: Settled on camera, three times.

criteria.test: Five minutes out of the apartment.
criteria.pass: Settled on camera, three times.

criteria.test: Fifteen minutes out of the apartment.
criteria.pass: Settled on camera, twice.

criteria.test: Thirty minutes.
criteria.pass: Settled on camera, twice.

criteria.test: An hour, with a Kong at the start.
criteria.pass: She sleeps through most of it, twice.

skills.title: Go to your bed
skills.age: From 12 to 14 weeks, once settle is working.
skills.why: Sending her somewhere is more useful than asking her to stop something. Doorbell, cooking, dinner, a delivery: a dog with a place to go does not need to be managed.
need: A defined mat or bed
Kibble

steps.do: Stand near the mat. The moment she steps on it, even one paw, mark and feed ON the mat.
steps.look: She comes back to it. Do not lure. Let her work out that the mat is what pays.

steps.do: Wait for all four paws, then for a sit, then for a down.
steps.look: She is offering a down on the mat.

steps.do: Add the word PLACE or BED as she is heading there.
steps.look: She goes on the word.

steps.do: Add distance. Send her from one step away, then two, then across the room.
steps.look: She goes from wherever you are.

steps.do: Add duration and distraction, exactly like stay. One at a time.
steps.look: She holds it while you cook.

wrong: Physically putting her on the mat. She has to choose it for the cue to mean anything.
Only using it when something stressful is happening, so the mat predicts stress.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: You are in another part of the room, the doorbell has just gone, and you say PLACE once.
criteria.pass: She goes and stays there, 8 out of 10 times.

skills.title: Hand target
skills.age: Any time. It is easy and it is unreasonably useful.
skills.why: A nose touch to your palm. It looks like a trick, and it is the most useful single behavior on this list after recall: it moves her without touching her, gets her past something scary, gets her onto scales, into a car, off a sofa, and gives a nervous dog something to do.
need: Kibble
Your hand

steps.do: Hold your apartment palm a few centimetres from her nose, off to one side. Say nothing.
steps.look: Curiosity makes her sniff it. The instant her nose touches, YES and feed.

steps.do: Move the hand around: left, right, higher, lower.
steps.look: She follows and touches.

steps.do: Add the word TOUCH just before you present the hand.
steps.look: She touches on the word.

steps.do: Add distance. Present the hand a step away, then two steps.
steps.look: She crosses the room to touch. This is now a mini-recall.

steps.do: Use it: to move her off the sofa, past a scary bin, onto the vet scales.
steps.look: It works in real situations.

wrong: Moving your hand toward her nose. Hold it still and let her come to it.
Rewarding a paw. Only pay the nose.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: Somewhere she has never done it before. Treats in a pocket or a closed pouch, not in your hand. One cue, no repeats.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 first-time responses. THIS is the answer to did she learn it. Not once. Not sometimes. Eight out of ten, cold, in a new place.

skills.title: Emergency recall
skills.age: From about 4 months, once normal recall is solid.
skills.why: A second, separate recall word that you never use casually and that is always paid with something extraordinary. Normal recall is for everyday. This one is for a car, an open gate, a dog running at her. It works precisely because it is rare.
need: A word you would never say otherwise. A whistle works well.
Something she gets at no other time: roast chicken, cheese, liver.

steps.do: At home, with her a meter away, make the sound. When she looks, deliver ten to fifteen seconds of continuous feeding, one piece after another, with genuine celebration.
steps.look: She is startled by how good it was.
steps.reps: Once a day for a week, then once a week.

steps.do: Increase distance and distraction very gradually, always with the same enormous payment.
steps.look: The sound produces an immediate sprint.

steps.do: Never use it for anything else. Not to come in from the garden, not for dinner, not to test it more than once a week.
steps.look: It stays loaded.

wrong: Using it more than once a week. Every casual use spends it.
Paying it with kibble. If it is not the best thing that happens to her all week, it is not an emergency recall.

criteria.test: The sound at home, a meter away.
criteria.pass: Immediate turn and approach, 6 out of 6.

criteria.test: Sound from another room while she is occupied.
criteria.pass: She comes, 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: On a long line, mid-sniff.
criteria.pass: Immediate turn, 5 out of 6.

criteria.test: On a long line, while a dog is visible in the distance.
criteria.pass: She comes, 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: Used at most once a week for three months, always paid enormously.
criteria.pass: Still produces a sprint after three months of near-disuse.

skills.title: Formal heel
skills.age: From 5 to 6 months, after loose leash walking is reliable.
skills.why: A precise position at your side, for crossing a busy road or squeezing past a crowd. Different from loose leash walking, which is what you want for 95 percent of a walk. Do not train heel before loose leash walking works; you will end up with a dog who only knows how to be glued to your leg or pull.
need: Chicken
A quiet space

steps.do: Stand still. Feed her repeatedly in the exact position you want: shoulder level with your leg.
steps.look: She learns the spot pays.

steps.do: Take one step. If she stays in position, mark and feed there. Build to three steps, then five.
steps.look: Position holds through movement.

steps.do: Add the word HEEL, and a release word to end it.
steps.look: She understands heel is a temporary job, not the whole walk.

steps.do: Add turns, then pace changes, then distractions.
steps.look: Position holds through change.

wrong: Using heel for the entire walk. It is mentally tiring and it removes the sniffing that makes a walk worth taking.
Training it before loose leash walking exists.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: Somewhere she has never done it before. Treats in a pocket or a closed pouch, not in your hand. One cue, no repeats.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 first-time responses. THIS is the answer to did she learn it. Not once. Not sometimes. Eight out of ten, cold, in a new place.

skills.title: Stand for examination
skills.age: From 4 months.
skills.why: A stationary stand while someone touches her. Every vet visit and every groom uses it, and it is the physical vocabulary for a dog who is easy to handle.
need: Kibble

steps.do: From a sit, hold food at nose height and move it straight forward. She stands to follow it. Mark the moment all four feet are down and still.
steps.look: She stands rather than walking on.

steps.do: Build duration: two seconds, five, ten.
steps.look: She holds.

steps.do: Add the word STAND, then add handling while she holds it.
steps.look: She stands while you run your hands over her.

wrong: Letting her sit as soon as she stops. Mark fast, before she folds.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: Somewhere she has never done it before. Treats in a pocket or a closed pouch, not in your hand. One cue, no repeats.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 first-time responses. THIS is the answer to did she learn it. Not once. Not sometimes. Eight out of ten, cold, in a new place.

skills.title: Greeting people without jumping
skills.age: From 4 months, and it never really stops.
skills.why: A golden retriever who jumps at 10 weeks is charming and at 30 kilos is not. The behavior is being trained right now, by everyone who bends down and makes a fuss of a jumping puppy.
need: Kibble by the door
Cooperative visitors
A lead for real arrivals

steps.do: Four on the floor. Nobody touches her, looks at her or speaks to her while any paw is off the ground.
steps.look: Attention arrives only when all four feet are down.

steps.do: The moment all four are down, mark and feed on the floor. Feeding low keeps her low.
steps.look: Food on the ground resets her position.

steps.do: Ask for a sit as a greeting behavior, once she has one.
steps.look: She offers a sit at people.

steps.do: Brief guests before they come in. Most people will undo this cheerfully if you let them.
steps.look: Consistency across everyone she meets.

wrong: Kneeing her, or pushing her off. To a social puppy that is contact, which is what she was asking for.
Letting some people allow it. One person who lets her jump keeps the behavior alive for everyone.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: A visitor arrives at the door, unbriefed, and she is off the leash.
criteria.pass: All four feet stay on the floor, 8 out of 10 arrivals.

skills.title: A real retrieve
skills.age: From 6 months. Informal fetch can start much earlier.
skills.sessions: 5 minutes, a few times a week.
skills.why: She is a retriever. This is the thing her breed was built for over two centuries, and a golden who never gets to use it is a golden with unspent energy. A trained retrieve is also enormously practical: it burns more energy in ten minutes than a half-hour walk, and it gives you something to do in a small flat on a bad day.
need: Two identical toys
A hallway or a long room

steps.do: Two-toy game. Throw one. The instant she picks it up, produce the second and make it exciting.
steps.look: She runs back to you with the first to get at the second. Do not chase her. Make the toy in your hand the interesting one.

steps.do: When she arrives, ask for DROP, then throw the second immediately as the reward.
steps.look: Bringing it back and dropping it is what starts the next throw.

steps.do: Add a hold: ask her to keep it in her mouth for a second before dropping.
steps.look: A clean hold rather than an instant spit.

steps.do: Add a wait before the send, so she does not break on the throw.
steps.look: She holds until released.

steps.do: Add distance, then hidden retrieves, then two thrown items retrieved in sequence.
steps.look: A structured, thinking retrieve rather than a frenzy.

wrong: Endless repetitive ball throwing. It is high-impact on joints, it builds obsessive arousal rather than fitness, and for a large breed still growing it is genuinely bad for her. Structured retrieves in small numbers beat forty throws.
Chasing her to get the toy back. That trains keep-away.
Starting formal work before her growth plates are closer to closed. Keep it flat, short and low-impact until then.
skills.note: Ask your vet when she can start higher-impact work. Growth plates in a large breed generally close somewhere around 12 to 18 months, and jumping and hard turns before then are a real concern.

criteria.test: With food visibly in your hand, she gets into position.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session.

criteria.test: Empty hand, same motion. She still does it. Reward comes from the other hand afterwards.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session. THIS is where most people get stuck, because they never fade the lure.

criteria.test: Say the word once, hands still, no hand signal. She does it.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 tries in one session, in the room you taught it in.

criteria.test: The verbal cue works in three different rooms, and once with a mild distraction: someone walking past, a toy on the floor, the TV on.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5 in each of three locations.

criteria.test: A hidden retrieve in an unfamiliar place: she goes out, finds it, brings it back, holds it, and gives it up on cue.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10 clean retrieves.

skills.title: Scent games and nosework
skills.age: Can start informally now. Formal work from 6 months.
skills.sessions: 10 minutes, two or three times a week.
skills.why: The highest value activity per minute for a dog in an apartment. Sniffing is genuinely tiring in a way walking is not, it lowers arousal, and it is something she can do brilliantly on a wet day when a walk is not appealing. For a retriever it is close to a biological need.
need: Cardboard boxes
Her kibble to start, a specific toy later
A room you can shut off

steps.do: FIND IT. Scatter ten pieces of kibble on a rug in front of her. Let her hoover.
steps.look: Nose goes down. That is all you need at the start.

steps.do: Hide pieces around a room while she waits outside. Let her in and say FIND IT.
steps.look: She searches systematically rather than randomly.

steps.do: Move to boxes. One box has food, five do not. Mark when she indicates the right one.
steps.look: She works the boxes rather than knocking them over.

steps.do: Progress to a single scented item hidden out of sight, higher up, or in another room.
steps.look: She tracks rather than scans.

steps.do: Formal nosework introduces a target odour and a trained indication. Worth a class.
steps.look: A clear, still indication at source.

wrong: Helping her. Point at nothing and let her solve it. The problem-solving is the exercise.
Making it too hard too early and letting her give up.

criteria.test: She puts her nose down and works a scatter feed without your help.
criteria.pass: Consistently.

criteria.test: Five hidden pieces in a room.
criteria.pass: Finds all five, 3 out of 4 attempts.

criteria.test: One baited box among six.
criteria.pass: Finds it, 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: A hidden item she has to work for, off the ground.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: A still, deliberate indication at source rather than pawing or grabbing.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

skills.title: Out-of-sight stay
skills.age: From 6 to 8 months, once stay is reliable.
skills.why: The genuinely difficult version. It underpins being left at a cafe table, waiting outside a shop, and staying put in an emergency.
need: An established stay at 30 seconds and 5 meters
A doorway

steps.do: Stay, walk to a doorway, step out of sight for ONE second, come straight back and reward.
steps.look: She holds. One second is not too small a step.

steps.do: Build the out-of-sight time irregularly: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 1.
steps.look: No predictable climb for her to anticipate.

steps.do: Change what she can hear. Move around out of sight, open a cupboard, run a tap.
steps.look: She holds through noise she cannot see the source of.

steps.do: Take it outdoors, on a long line for safety, never off-leash in an unfenced space.
steps.look: It holds in a real environment.

wrong: Going too far too fast. The failure here is not a broken stay, it is a puppy who learns that you disappearing is worth worrying about.
Practising it when she is already unsettled about being alone. Fix that first.

criteria.test: Out of sight for one second.
criteria.pass: 6 out of 6.

criteria.test: Out of sight for ten seconds.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: Out of sight for a minute.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: A minute out of sight with household noise.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: Thirty seconds out of sight outdoors, on a long line.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

skills.title: Recall off something exciting
skills.age: From 6 months, and it is never finished.
skills.why: Coming back from a sniff is a different problem from coming back from a squirrel. This is the difference between a dog you can let off leash and a dog you cannot, and it is built deliberately, in a graded ladder, not discovered in a park.
need: A long line
The best food you have
A helper

steps.do: Build a distraction ladder, written down, from easiest to hardest. Food on the floor. A rolling ball. A person she likes. A dog at 50 meters. A dog at 20. A dog at 5. A squirrel.
steps.look: You know exactly what the next step is rather than guessing.

steps.do: Start at rung one, on the long line, at a distance where she can still hear you. Call once. Pay enormously.
steps.look: She turns. If she does not, you are too close to the distraction. Increase distance, do not increase volume.

steps.do: Move one rung at a time, over weeks. Never skip.
steps.look: Steady progress.

steps.do: Practice recalling her AWAY from something and then releasing her back to it, where it is safe.
steps.look: Coming back does not reliably end the good thing, so there is nothing to weigh up.

wrong: Testing it off-leash to see if it works. If you are testing, you already know it might fail, and every failure trains the opposite.
Increasing your volume instead of your distance. Shouting does not make a distraction less interesting.

criteria.test: Recall past food on the floor, on a line.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10.

criteria.test: Recall off a rolling ball.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10.

criteria.test: Recall away from a person she wants to greet.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10.

criteria.test: Recall with a dog visible 30 meters away.
criteria.pass: 8 out of 10.

criteria.test: Recall with a dog 10 meters away, on a long line.
criteria.pass: 9 out of 10 before you ever consider off-leash.

skills.title: Trick chains
skills.age: Any time after the foundations. Genuinely useful, not just fun.
skills.why: Tricks are not frivolous. They are the cheapest way to build a dog who enjoys learning, they burn mental energy on days when physical exercise is limited, and chaining several behaviours together teaches her to keep working through a sequence without a reward after every step, which is exactly what real-world obedience requires.
need: Kibble
A marker word that is working well

steps.do: Pick single tricks she can already nearly do: spin, paw, bow, roll over, back up, chin rest.
steps.look: Each one trained the same way: shape or lure, fade the lure, name it last.

steps.do: Introduce shaping: mark tiny approximations of a behavior with no lure at all.
steps.look: She starts offering behavior to see what pays. That is a dog who has learned how to learn.

steps.do: Chain two known tricks with one reward at the end.
steps.look: She works through both without stopping.

steps.do: Build to three and four behavior chains.
steps.look: Sustained work on a single reward.

wrong: Cueing a chain she has not learned as separate pieces.
Chin rest is worth prioritising over the showy ones. It is genuinely useful for eye drops, ear cleaning and vet handling.

criteria.test: Three separate tricks on verbal cue alone.
criteria.pass: 5 out of 6 each.

criteria.test: She offers behavior when you stand still with food and say nothing.
criteria.pass: She experiments rather than waiting.

criteria.test: Two behaviours, one reward.
criteria.pass: 4 out of 5.

criteria.test: Four behaviours, one reward at the end.
criteria.pass: 3 out of 4.

criteria.test: She learns a brand new trick in under three sessions.
criteria.pass: Twice, with two different tricks.

skills.title: Talking buttons
skills.age: Not yet. From about six months, and only once ten words are genuinely solid.
skills.sessions: One button. Thirty seconds a day, attached to something that already happens.
skills.why: Worth knowing what the research actually says, because the box overstates it and the internet dismisses it. Rossano's group at UC San Diego has published the first real studies on soundboard dogs. In 2024 they showed that button presses are non-random and non-imitative, including meaningful two-button combinations like outside plus potty, and separately that dogs respond appropriately when a HUMAN presses a word button, which rules out the dog simply reading the person. So it is real: word comprehension and deliberate requesting. It is not language, grammar or conversation, and she will never tell you her hip hurts. Treat it as a good enrichment game for a clever retriever and a bad substitute for training.
need: ONE button. The other seven stay in the box.
A word she already responds to reliably
Her marker, and a lot of patience

steps.do: Wait. She is ten weeks old and does not have a charged marker yet. Everything on this board needs her to already know what words mean. The box goes in a cupboard until about six months.
steps.look: Nothing. This step is you not doing it yet.

steps.do: When you do start: one button, and NOT outside or potty. The door bell already owns that meaning and she cannot have two channels for one need. Start with PLAY.
steps.look: Record it in a flat, ordinary voice, the same voice every time. Not a silly voice, because you will not reproduce it.

steps.do: YOU press it, and then immediately do the thing. Press PLAY, then play. Every single time, for a fortnight, before she is ever expected to press it.
steps.look: This is charging, exactly like the marker. The sound has to mean the event before it can mean a request.

steps.do: Make it available. Put it on a non-slip mat on the floor, where she already is when she wants that thing.
steps.look: She investigates it. Do not lure her onto it and do not shape a paw press with food.

steps.do: Honour every press for the first month, including the inconvenient ones and the accidental ones.
steps.look: A button that works sometimes is a button she abandons.

steps.do: A second button only once she uses the first one deliberately, which means she presses it and then looks at YOU rather than at the button. That takes weeks, not days.
steps.look: The look back is the whole test. Without it she has learned that pressing makes a noise.
steps.reps: One new word at a time.

steps.do: Never test her. No lining buttons up and asking her to choose.
steps.look: Testing turns a game into a chore, and that is the fastest way to kill it.

wrong: An OUTSIDE or POTTY button while she is using the door bell. Pick one channel and stay on it.
Eight buttons on day one. She learns that pressing things makes noise, and nothing else, and it is hard to come back from.
Different voices for the same word, or three people each recording their own. One person, one recording, one tone.
Reading meaning into a press you wanted to see. She pressed OUTSIDE and then vomited does not mean she told you she felt sick.
Using it instead of training. It is a hobby you do together. It is not a route around the marker, recall or leave it, and if you are skipping those for this, you have the trade backwards.
skills.note: This is the one item on the list she does not need. Nothing goes wrong if the box stays shut for good. It is a nice thing to do with a clever dog and an owner who enjoys it, and the honest cost is your consistency, which is the same currency recall and leave it are paid in.

criteria.test: You have pressed PLAY and then played, every time, for two weeks.
criteria.pass: You have done it consistently. There is nothing to see from her yet, and that is correct.

criteria.test: She presses it and then looks at you rather than at the button.
criteria.pass: Three separate times, unprompted.

criteria.test: She presses PLAY when she wants to play, not when she wants food or the door.
criteria.pass: Clearly more right than wrong over two weeks.

criteria.test: One new button at a time, each charged the same way.
criteria.pass: Each used in the right context 4 presses out of 5 before the next one is added.

criteria.test: Two buttons pressed together in a way that makes sense.
criteria.pass: It happens on its own. If you engineered it, it does not count.

skills.title: Canine Good Citizen
skills.age: Typically from 6 months.
skills.why: An external, structured target with someone qualified watching you. Worth doing not for the certificate but because it forces you to proof everything in a room full of dogs and strangers, which is the one thing you cannot manufacture at home.
need: A class near you
Her vaccinations complete

steps.do: Find a class that is explicitly reward-based. Ask what they do when a dog gets it wrong. If the answer involves a correction, a check chain, or the word dominance, find another class.
steps.look: A trainer who can explain their method without jargon.

steps.do: The test covers: accepting a friendly stranger, sitting politely for petting, appearance and grooming, walking on a loose leash, walking through a crowd, sit and down on cue and staying in place, coming when called, reaction to another dog, reaction to a distraction, and supervised separation.
steps.look: Every one of those is already on this list. The class is proofing, not new material.

wrong: Choosing a class on convenience alone. The method matters more than the location.

criteria.test: You have found and started a reward-based class.
criteria.pass: Attending weekly.

criteria.test: Five of the ten test items pass in class conditions.
criteria.pass: Assessed in class.

criteria.test: All ten in class conditions.
criteria.pass: Assessed in class.

criteria.test: The actual test.
criteria.pass: Passed.

criteria.test: Still holds three months after the test, outside class.
criteria.pass: Spot-checked.
